title: 用 Python 构建生成式 UI：Jeremiah Lowin 讲 Prefab 与 FastMCP
author: AI Engineer
content:
Brief Description

Jeremiah Lowin explains how MCP apps move an agent interaction beyond text-only tool results and why that creates a practical UI problem for Python-focused developers. He introduces Prefab, a constrained, component-based UI framework for FastMCP, and shows how its Python DSL, serializable UI protocol, interactive tools, full applications, and generative UI workflow make rich MCP experiences possible without asking developers to build a conventional frontend from scratch.

Table of Contents

  • MCP apps and the UI opportunity
  • Designing for Python developers and enterprise tasks
  • Prefab's component model and Python DSL
  • Interactive FastMCP tools and full applications
  • Generative UI and the protocol behind it

MCP apps and the UI opportunity

MCP servers are a useful way to add functions and business logic to agents, but a normal MCP request-response cycle has no direct connection between the user and the server. A user asks an agent for something, the agent calls a tool on an MCP server, receives the result in its context window, and forms a response. Everything passes through the agent.

MCP apps extend that model. The agent can still invoke a tool, but instead of sending the result back only to the agent, the tool can deliver HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to the user as a complete UI. That UI can be custom, branded, and interactive. The agent facilitates the interaction, while the person can work directly with the application.

This makes experiences such as booking a restaurant table, changing an airline seat, or interacting with a schedule possible in a more natural way. An upcoming MCP extension can also let the agent interact with the app, which opens further possibilities, such as a visual game where the person and the agent both make moves.

Designing for Python developers and enterprise tasks

Lowin maintains FastMCP, a popular way to build MCP servers. When MCP apps became possible, the question was how to make them accessible to FastMCP users, who are largely Python engineers. Building interactive, attractive, useful frontends for them should not mean trying to force the entire frontend ecosystem into Python or pretending that React can simply be shipped as Python.

The design becomes clearer by considering what these developers actually need. Many work in enterprises, where their primary job is sharing information across an organization and collecting information from it. They generally do not need fully branded consumer-grade interfaces. They need practical surfaces for tables, forms, and charts.

That constraint led to Prefab, an open-source, deliberately scoped UI-building framework for delivering agent-mediated interfaces. Its goal is not arbitrary frontend development. It is to compose well-designed components into structured interfaces for the tasks MCP app developers commonly need to solve.

Prefab's component model and Python DSL

Prefab can produce a familiar interactive card, such as a small interface that updates when someone enters a name, but the code that generates it is entirely Python. The combination feels unusual at first. The useful insight is that composing a frontend in Python can feel natural when the problem is scoped correctly: developers are not creating a frontend from scratch, but assembling a frontend from world-class components with guardrails that preserve the user experience.

The framework uses context managers as its main DSL. In the same reductive way that FastMCP can be described as using a Python decorator to build an MCP server, Prefab can be described as using a context manager to build an entire UI. Nesting component context managers produces the same structure as the rendered interface, so the code makes the hierarchy visible when read.

Each rendered component is a class that can be instantiated and parameterized, including with CSS classes. Reactive variables provide client-side interactivity and data binding between components. A reactive value can be referenced, formatted, or used as a name in the Python code, and Prefab compiles it into the corresponding JavaScript behavior.

Under the hood, the Python DSL builds a declarative representation of the UI. That representation is serialized into a JSON protocol, and a React application hosted as the MCP app renders it. The key asset is the serializable representation, not Python itself: it can be generated by an agent, sent to an agent, or generated by a person and modified by an agent. The Python DSL emerged as a compact and pleasant way to author that representation.

Prefab's own documentation demonstrates the approach. It ships roughly 130 to 140 components, and the documentation is rendered in Prefab itself. A data table in the documentation is live, and its Python example can be opened in a playground, edited, and immediately reflected in the UI. The approach makes more sense when treated as UI composition rather than unrestricted frontend construction.

Interactive FastMCP tools and full applications

The first use of Prefab in an MCP server is an interactive tool. A normal FastMCP tool is a decorated Python function that returns information to the agent. To make it interactive, the function returns a Prefab component instead of a Python dictionary. Returning a data-table component, for example, lets FastMCP detect that the result is an MCP app and set up the HTML, JavaScript, CSS, and rendering needed for the user to see it.

In practice, a request such as showing a team directory can produce an interactive data table with searching, filtering, sorting, and pagination. The developer only returns the table class. The interface can be extended incrementally: importing a grid and a pie chart, then composing both with a context manager, creates a chart next to the table. This follows a framework principle of one line of code producing one visible, meaningful change.

Prefab also supports fully client-side interactions without handwritten JavaScript. Controls can share a reactive attribute so that values and text update together automatically. For more complete experiences, a FastMCP app can have a class, one or more app.ui functions that return the base Prefab UI, and optional app.tool methods that act as backend methods callable from the interface.

File upload illustrates why a full app matters. Because an agent normally has access to the MCP server, directly uploading a file through a conventional tool can turn into an expensive copy-and-paste operation: the agent receives a large body of text and has to relay it into the server. An MCP app can present an upload interface so a person drags in a file and it goes directly to the server, bypassing the agent. FastMCP provides this as a concise built-in component alongside other useful tools.

Generative UI and the protocol behind it

The final example is a fully generative UI. Lowin demonstrates giving Claude an instruction to begin streaming an interesting interface. The exposed tool accepts the serialized UI protocol used by Prefab. As the agent streams the representation over the wire, the system renders whatever it has in real time, repairs the JSON as needed, and continues rendering. The agent can create an interface without the developer specifying every UI detail; a supplied skill tells it how to write the UI.

The architecture evolved after experimentation. The original demo streamed the JSON representation, which would be rendered in the React application. The team found that the Python representation of a UI was about 70 percent smaller than its JSON representation. The newer approach streams Python, executes it in a sandbox, converts it into JSON on the server, and renders the result. The outcome is substantially better token efficiency, cost, and latency while retaining the same overall workflow.

Prefab is available through its documentation and GitHub library, and is already integrated into FastMCP. Developers using a recent FastMCP version can install the optional addition, import components, return them from their tools, and begin experimenting with MCP apps.
aiSummary: Jeremiah Lowin 介绍 Prefab 如何让 FastMCP 开发者通过 Python 组合交互式 MCP 应用，借助可序列化的 UI 协议、响应式组件和沙箱化生成式 UI 工作流，避免从零搭建传统前端。
oneSentenceSummary: Jeremiah Lowin 介绍 Prefab 如何让 FastMCP 开发者通过 Python 组合交互式 MCP 应用，借助可序列化的 UI 协议、响应式组件和沙箱化生成式 UI 工作流，避免从零搭建传统前端。
summary: Jeremiah Lowin 将 Prefab 定位为面向 Python 开发者的受限 UI 框架，用于通过 FastMCP 构建 MCP 应用。他先指出普通工具调用的局限：结果只经由智能体上下文返回；而 MCP 应用能把交互界面直接交给用户。Prefab 借助 Python 上下文管理器和响应式变量组合表格、表单、图表和完整应用，再将声明式 UI 序列化并由 React 客户端渲染。演讲区分了交互式工具结果与拥有服务端方法的完整应用，并以文件上传说明用户可直连服务器，避免让智能体转发大段内容。生成式 UI 示例则让智能体直接使用该协议，一边创建一边呈现界面。实现后来从流式传输 JSON 改为流式传输沙箱中的 Python；讲者表示，后者在保持渲染模型不变的前提下，能显著降低 token 消耗和延迟。

mainPoints.point: MCP 应用让交互不再局限于文本工具结果
mainPoints.explanation: MCP 工具不必只把结果送回智能体上下文，也可以向用户交付可交互的 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript 界面，同时仍由智能体协助完成任务。

mainPoints.point: Prefab 为 Python 开发者限定了前端组合范围
mainPoints.explanation: 它并不宣称用 Python 替代无限制的前端开发，而是提供带有体验约束的组件，供开发者用上下文管理器组合企业场景常见的表格、表单和图表。

mainPoints.point: 可序列化协议才是核心抽象
mainPoints.explanation: Python 类和响应式变量先构建声明式 UI 表示，再序列化为 JSON 并由 React 应用渲染，因此人和智能体都能创作或修改同一套界面模型。

mainPoints.point: 完整 MCP 应用可绕开由智能体中转数据的成本
mainPoints.explanation: 应用拥有 UI 与后端方法后，用户可以把文件直接上传给服务器，不必让智能体接收并通过普通工具调用转发大段文本。

mainPoints.point: 流式传输沙箱化 Python 可提升生成式 UI 效率
mainPoints.explanation: 最初方案流式传输 JSON；团队发现 Python 表示约小 70%，于是先在沙箱中执行流式 Python 再渲染，在保留工作流的同时降低 token 成本和延迟。

keyQuotes: 他们需要的是适用于表格、表单和图表的实用界面。
真正关键的资产是可序列化的表示，而不是 Python 本身：它可以由智能体生成、发送给智能体，或由人生成后再由智能体修改。
团队发现，UI 的 Python 表示比 JSON 表示小约 70%。
